+# Why Mrs Beech's docket names a bottle of cordial
+
+## What happens
+
+`cli.py make-up` reads `orders.json` and loops over `book["orders"]` in the
+order the three orders appear: Mrs Beech, then Col. Ashton, then Dr Vane.
+
+For each order it calls `hampers.make_up(order["customer"], order.get("wants"))`
+and then, still inside the same loop iteration, walks `order.get("extras", [])`
+and calls `hampers.add_extra(hamper, item)` for each one. Each made-up hamper
+is appended to a list, `made`. Only *after* the loop over all three orders has
+finished does `cli.py` loop over `made` a second time and print a docket for
+each hamper, via `docket.docket(hamper)`.
+
+Order by order:
+
+1. **Mrs Beech** has no `wants` and no `extras`. `hampers.make_up("Mrs Beech", None)`
+   is called. Since `wants` is `None`, `hampers.py` takes the `else` branch and
+   sets `contents = STANDARD` — not a copy of `STANDARD`, but the very list
+   object `STANDARD` itself. Her hamper dict is `{"customer": "Mrs Beech",
+   "contents": STANDARD}`. No extras run, so nothing is appended yet.
+
+2. **Col. Ashton** also has no `wants`, so he too gets `contents = STANDARD` —
+   the *same* list object again. His order does have `extras: ["a bottle of
+   cordial"]`, so `hampers.add_extra(hamper, "a bottle of cordial")` runs,
+   which does `hamper["contents"].append(item)`. Because his `contents` is
+   `STANDARD` itself, this mutates the module-level `STANDARD` list in place.
+   From this point on, `STANDARD` is
+   `["a quarter of tea", "a bag of sugar", "a fruit cake", "a jar of
+   marmalade", "a bottle of cordial"]` — five items, permanently, for the
+   rest of the run.
+
+3. **Dr Vane** has his own `wants`, so `hampers.make_up` takes the `if wants
+   is not None` branch and builds `contents = list(wants)` — a fresh list,
+   unrelated to `STANDARD`. His hamper is untouched by anything that happened
+   to Mrs Beech's or Col. Ashton's.
+
+Only now does `cli.py` print the dockets, reading each hamper's `contents`
+as it stands *at print time*, not as it stood when `make_up` first built it.
+Mrs Beech's hamper dict still holds a reference to `STANDARD` — the same
+object Col. Ashton's order mutated — so her docket enumerates all five
+items, cordial included, and `docket.py`'s `len(hamper["contents"])` reports
+5 item(s).
+
+## Why it comes out that way
+
+- **`hampers.STANDARD` is one shared list object, not a template.** It is
+  defined once at module scope (`hampers.py:12-17`) and is never copied
+  before being handed out.
+- **`make_up`'s standard branch aliases rather than copies:**
+  `contents = STANDARD` (`hampers.py:29`) binds `contents` — and hence
+  `hamper["contents"]` — directly to that one shared object. Contrast with
+  the bespoke branch, `contents = list(wants)` (`hampers.py:27`), which
+  *does* copy, which is exactly why Dr Vane's hamper is immune.
+- **`add_extra` mutates in place:** `hamper["contents"].append(item)`
+  (`hampers.py:35`) appends to whatever list object `contents` happens to
+  be, with no check for whether that object is private to this hamper or
+  shared.
+- **Every standard order in a run shares the same object.** Mrs Beech's and
+  Col. Ashton's hampers are `is`-identical in their `"contents"` list,
+  because both took the aliasing branch against the same `STANDARD` global.
+  An extra added via one standard customer's order is, mechanically, added
+  to every standard customer's hamper — past, present, and future in that
+  run — because there is really only one list.
+- **The book is made up entirely before any docket is written**
+  (`cli.py:32-43`, and the comment there says so directly: "the whole book
+  is made up first and the dockets are written out together at the end").
+  Docket text is not fixed at the moment `make_up`/`add_extra` run for a
+  given customer; it is read off `hamper["contents"]` later, at print time.
+  So it doesn't matter that Mrs Beech's hamper was built before Col.
+  Ashton's extra was added — her docket is written after his mutation, and
+  by then the shared list already carries the cordial.
+- **Order in the book matters.** The cordial lands on `STANDARD` during Col.
+  Ashton's turn, which comes after Mrs Beech's in `orders.json`. Every
+  standard hamper made up before that point in the loop is affected too
+  (because it's the same object), and so is every standard hamper made up
+  after it in the same run, since the mutation is permanent for the process.
+- **Dr Vane's docket is correct and unaffected** because his order carries
+  `wants`, so his hamper never touches `STANDARD` at all — `list(wants)`
+  gives him a private list from the start.
+
+## Boundaries and edge behavior
+
+- **Every standard order in the same `make-up` run is contaminated
+  together**, not just the one that comes right after an order with
+  extras. If a fourth, fifth, or sixth customer also ordered the plain
+  standard hamper, their dockets would show the cordial too — including
+  standard orders listed *before* Col. Ashton's in the book, since the
+  aliasing happens at `make_up` time but the mutation is read at print
+  time, after the whole book is made up. This run's book only has one
+  other standard order (Mrs Beech's), so only one docket besides Col.
+  Ashton's own shows the effect, but the code does not limit the damage to
+  "the next" standard order — it is scoped to "every hamper dict currently
+  pointing at `STANDARD`," which in this run is both of them.
+- **A second `extras` entry, or a second order with `extras`, compounds
+  further**: each `add_extra` call against a standard hamper appends to the
+  same shared list again, so a later standard docket in the same run could
+  show items added by more than one other customer's order — nothing in
+  the code de-duplicates or scopes an extra to the order that requested it.
+- **The corruption persists only for the lifetime of one `STANDARD` list
+  object.** Since `STANDARD` is a module-level list re-created fresh each
+  time the `hampers` module is imported, a *separate* invocation of `python
+  cli.py make-up` starts clean — the bug is per-run, not persisted to
+  `orders.json` or any file on disk. Nothing in this repository writes
+  hamper state back out except the printed dockets, and the repository is
+  left exactly as found by running it.
+- **Bespoke orders (`wants` present) are categorically safe** from this
+  mechanism, because `list(wants)` always allocates a new list; nothing a
+  bespoke order's own `extras` do can leak into another hamper, and nothing
+  another order does can leak into a bespoke hamper's contents.
+- **The `book` subcommand is unaffected.** It prints straight from the JSON
+  order records (`order.get("extras", [])`) rather than from any hamper
+  built by `hampers.make_up`, so it always reports Mrs Beech's order
+  accurately as the plain standard hamper with no extras — the discrepancy
+  is confined to `make-up`'s hamper-then-docket path.
+- **What the repository does not settle:** nothing in the code, comments,
+  or `README.md` states whether the shared `STANDARD` list is an
+  intentional shortcut or an oversight. The docstring in `hampers.py`
+  ("What the standard hamper holds. Every standard order is packed to this
+  list") is consistent with either reading — "this list" could mean "this
+  fixed set of items" (the evidently intended meaning, given the module's
+  own framing that "it is the same hamper for everybody") or, as the code
+  actually behaves, "this one Python list object." Whether the intended fix
+  is `list(STANDARD)` in `make_up`, a copy inside `add_extra`, or something
+  else is not decidable from the repository as it stands — it is a
+  judgment call about intent, not a fact the code discloses.
output:
Only `ANSWER.md` was added; all other files are untouched.

**Root cause, in short:** `hampers.py`'s `make_up` gives every standard order the same list object (`contents = STANDARD`, no copy), while bespoke orders get a fresh `list(wants)`. `add_extra` mutates that list in place. Since `cli.py` builds *all* hampers before printing *any* docket, Col. Ashton's `"a bottle of cordial"` extra — appended to the shared `STANDARD` object — is visible on Mrs Beech's hamper too by the time her docket is written, giving her 5 items instead of 4. Dr Vane's bespoke order is immune because his list was never shared. Full trace, decisions, and edge behavior are in `ANSWER.md`.

+# Fifty fathoms of hawser-laid rope
+
+## What happens
+
+The clerk types `ropewalk order <customer> 50 hawser`. `cli.py` parses this
+into the `order` subcommand, loads the yard file with `stores.load`, and
+calls `counter.take_order(yard, customer, 50, "hawser")` — the one place an
+asking becomes a walk (`counter.py:31`).
+
+`take_order` first checks the asking against what the counter knows how to
+do: `"hawser"` must be a key of `STRANDS` (it is — three strands,
+`counter.py:18`), and `50` must be at least one fathom. Then it turns the
+asking into a length the walk can actually lay:
+
+- `hauls_for(50)` computes `-(-50 // 20)`. Fifty fathoms is two and a half
+  hauls of twenty, and floor-division of a negated numerator is the
+  standard way to round up without importing anything: `-50 // 20 == -3`,
+  negated is `3`. Three hauls.
+- `walked = 3 * 20 = 60` fathoms — the order is made up to a whole haul,
+  not cut down.
+
+`counter.py` hands this on to `walk.walk_out(yard, 60, 3, "hawser")`
+(`walk.py:22`). The walk works out what the rack owes it before it takes
+anything down: `yarn_for(60, 3) = 60 * 3 = 180` fathoms — the walked length,
+taken off the rack once per strand of a hawser lay. It checks
+`stores.on_hand(yard) >= 180` as a single up-front test, then calls
+`stores.draw(yard, 180)`.
+
+`draw` (`stores.py:42`) takes yarn off the *front* of the rack, in the order
+bundles were put up: it looks at `yard["bundles"][0]`, records its mark,
+and either consumes it whole and pops it off (if the bundle holds no more
+than what's still needed) or subtracts what's needed from it and leaves it
+sitting at the front, partly used (if the bundle holds more than what's
+left). It repeats until 180 fathoms have been drawn, returning the list of
+marks every bundle it touched carried, in the order it touched them.
+
+Back in `walk_out`, this becomes a coil:
+`{"fathoms": 60, "lay": "hawser", "yarn_fathoms": 180, "bundles": [...marks...]}`.
+Back in `take_order`, the coil and the *original* asking — 50, not 60 — go
+to `book.enter(yard, customer, 50, coil)` (`book.py:18`).
+
+`enter` first calls `take_serial`, which reads `yard["next_serial"]`,
+increments it in the yard, and uses the value it read to build the tag:
+`f"RW-{serial}"`. It then appends one dispatch entry to
+`yard["dispatches"]`:
+
+```
+{
+    "tag": "RW-<n>",
+    "customer": <customer>,
+    "asked": 50,
+    "walked": 60,
+    "lay": "hawser",
+    "price_pence": 60 * 9,   # PENCE_PER_FATHOM["hawser"]
+}
+```
+
+`enter` returns the tag; `take_order` returns it unchanged; `cli.py` prints
+it and then calls `stores.save(yard, args.yard)`, which serializes the
+whole yard — rack, book, and counter — back to `yard.json`. The rack is
+now 180 fathoms lighter, the book has one more line, and `next_serial` has
+advanced by one. Nothing else in the file changed.
+
+## Why it comes out that way
+
+- **The counter, not the walk, decides length.** `HAUL_FATHOMS = 20` and
+  `hauls_for` live in `counter.py`; `walk.py` only ever sees a fathom
+  figure it is told to lay. The comment at the top of `counter.py` is
+  explicit about this: the walk "cannot lay a part of a haul," so the
+  rounding-up has to happen before the walk is asked for anything.
+
+- **Rounding up, never down.** `hauls_for` uses ceiling division
+  specifically because "the counter does not send a customer away short"
+  (`counter.py:26`) — fifty fathoms asked becomes sixty walked, ten
+  fathoms of margin the customer did not ask for but will be charged for.
+
+- **The book bills the walk, not the asking.** `book.enter`'s docstring
+  states the rule directly: "every fathom on the tag was laid, and the
+  book charges for what was walked" (`book.py:23`). `price_pence` is
+  `coil["fathoms"] * PENCE_PER_FATHOM[lay]` — `coil["fathoms"]` is the
+  *walked* 60, never the asked 50. The entry keeps `asked` too, so the
+  gap between what was requested and what was billed is visible on the
+  book, not hidden.
+
+- **A strand multiplies consumption, not the coil's length.** `yarn_for`
+  (`walk.py:16`) is `fathoms * strands` because "every strand runs the
+  full length of the walk," so a length "takes its own fathoms off the
+  rack once per strand." Sixty walked fathoms of a three-strand lay draw
+  180 fathoms of yarn — three times as much yarn as rope comes out. This
+  is also why `hawser` (3 strands) and `shroud` (4 strands) draw
+  differently for the same walked length; the lay is not just a label,
+  it is the multiplier stored alongside it in `STRANDS`.
+
+- **The whole draw is checked before any of it happens.** `walk_out`
+  computes `needed` and checks it against `stores.on_hand(yard)` in one
+  shot before calling `stores.draw` at all (`walk.py:29-35`), so "an
+  order the rack cannot cover is refused here, whole, and the rack is
+  left exactly as it stood." Nothing is drawn and put back; the check
+  simply happens before the draw, not during it.
+
+- **Draw order is FIFO and mutates bundles in place.** `stores.draw`
+  always looks at index `0` and either shrinks that bundle's `fathoms` in
+  place (leaving it at the front, still oldest) or pops it entirely
+  before moving to the new index `0`. Bundles put up later
+  (`stores.put_up` appends to the end of the list) are never touched
+  while an earlier bundle still has yarn on it. A coil's `bundles` list
+  is therefore the marks of the oldest yarn on hand, in the order it was
+  consumed, with each mark appearing at most once per draw.
+
+- **The serial is only spent on a coil that actually left.** `take_serial`
+  is called from inside `book.enter`, which `take_order` only reaches
+  after `walk.walk_out` has already succeeded (drawn its yarn without
+  raising). A refused order — bad lay, fathoms under one, or insufficient
+  stock — never reaches `book.enter`, so `next_serial` never advances and
+  no tag is ever skipped for a failed asking.
+
+- **One file, one load, one save.** `stores.py`'s module docstring frames
+  loading and saving as "the ends of every command"; `cli.py` loads once
+  at the top of `main` and, for the mutating commands (`order`,
+  `put-up`), saves once at the bottom. Everything in between — counter,
+  walk, book — works on the same in-memory `yard` dict, so the rack draw
+  and the book entry for one order are written out together or not at
+  all from the CLI's point of view.
+
+## Boundaries and edge behavior
+
+- **Insufficient stock refuses the whole order, cleanly.** If the rack
+  holds less than the 180 fathoms of yarn a 50-fathom hawser order needs,
+  `walk_out` raises `ValueError` naming both figures (`walk.py:31-34`)
+  before `stores.draw` is ever called — the rack is untouched, no serial
+  is taken, no dispatch is written. `stores.draw` carries the identical
+  check again (`stores.py:50`), but by the time a call from
+  `counter.take_order` could reach it, `walk_out` has already made the
+  same test pass; that second check only matters to a caller that calls
+  `stores.draw` directly, bypassing `walk_out`, which no code in this
+  repository does.
+
+- **An unrigged lay is refused before the rack is even consulted.**
+  `"cable"` or any other string not in `STRANDS` fails `take_order`'s own
+  check (`counter.py:36-37`) before `hauls_for` or `walk_out` run at all.
+  The CLI narrows this further with `choices=sorted(counter.STRANDS)`
+  (`cli.py:17`), so an invalid lay never even reaches `take_order` when
+  the order comes in through `cli.py` — the check in `counter.py` is
+  reachable only from a caller that constructs an order outside the CLI
+  (there is no other caller in this repository, so it is currently
+  unexercised but not dead: it is the boundary a non-CLI caller would
+  hit).
+
+- **An asking of zero or fewer fathoms is refused at the counter, not the
+  rack.** `take_order` checks `fathoms < 1` itself (`counter.py:38-39`);
+  it never reaches `hauls_for` or the rack. `stores.put_up` enforces the
+  same floor on deliveries (`stores.py:32-33`), but that is a separate
+  check guarding a separate operation — a delivery of yarn, not an
+  order for rope.
+
+- **A part-haul is never cut down, only made up — with no ceiling of its
+  own.** There's no maximum order size named anywhere: `hauls_for` will
+  happily compute an arbitrarily large number of hauls for an
+  arbitrarily large asking, and the only limit an order meets is however
+  much yarn happens to be on the rack. Nothing in the code speaks to
+  whether the walk itself has a capacity per run; "one haul is one trip
+  down the walk" is stated as a fact about timing, not as a constraint
+  the code enforces or even tracks (there is no notion of walks-in-
+  progress, only fathoms drawn and coils recorded).
+
+- **A bundle drawn down to zero fathoms is not distinguished from one
+  with a positive remainder — except by being removed.** `draw`'s
+  branch is `bundle["fathoms"] > left`; a bundle whose remaining
+  fathoms exactly equal what's left takes the `else` branch and is
+  popped, same as a bundle with too little. There is no bundle left
+  behind holding `0` fathoms; the rack never contains an empty bundle
+  the way the book contains a zero-fathom dispatch. Whether a bundle
+  that has been fully drawn should still be remembered anywhere (it
+  isn't — once popped, its mark survives only inside whatever coil's
+  `bundles` list it was drawn into) is not a question the code answers.
+
+- **The twist is named and then set aside.** `walk.py`'s docstring says
+  plainly that "the twist takes up nothing here: the walk lays slack and
+  the stretch comes out on the hooks" — i.e. `yarn_for` is a flat
+  `fathoms * strands` with no shrinkage or take-up factor for the
+  laying-up process itself. Whether real rope-laying loses length to
+  twist is a question the repository raises only to declare out of
+  scope; nothing here computes or records such a loss, and no field in
+  the yard file has anywhere to put one.
+
+- **Reads (`rack`, `book`) never save; only `order` and `put-up` do.**
+  `cli.py`'s `rack` and `book` branches `return` before reaching
+  `stores.save` (`cli.py:37`, `cli.py:45`). This is consistent with
+  those commands touching nothing in the loaded `yard` dict, but it also
+  means the save step is positional — tied to `cli.py`'s control flow,
+  not to whether the yard was actually mutated by whatever runs before
+  it. A future read-only command that forgot to `return` would silently
+  start rewriting the file; the current code avoids this by every
+  read-only branch returning early, not by any check on whether a
+  mutation occurred.
+
+- **Persistence is whole-file and not atomic.** `stores.save` does one
+  `Path.write_text` of the entire yard, and `stores.load` does one
+  `Path.read_text` plus `json.loads`. There is no temp-file-and-rename,
+  no locking, and no schema check on load beyond assuming the three keys
+  (`bundles`, `dispatches`, `next_serial`) are present and well-formed.
+  What happens to a hand-edited or partially-written `yard.json`, or to
+  two clerks running the CLI against the same file at once, is not a
+  question this repository answers — there is exactly one reader and
+  one writer assumed, both within a single `main()` call.
output: I traced the fifty-fathom hawser order through `counter.py` → `walk.py` → `stores.py` → `book.py` → back to `cli.py`'s save, and wrote the three-section explanation to `ANSWER.md`. No repository files were modified.

+# Why the town board and the quay board disagree
+
+## What happens
+
+`python cli.py town` and `python cli.py quay` both start the same way. `cli.py`
+loads the one book (`shedbook.load`), which hands back exactly the JSON that's
+on disk — `book.json` holds four workings, two from each end, each kept as a
+dict with `car`, `end`, and `leaves` fields where `leaves` is a string: `"9:40"`
+and `"10:05"` for both town and quay.
+
+For the town command, `cli.py` calls `boards.town_board(book)`. That function
+filters the workings down to the ones whose `end` is `"town"` — car 7 at
+`"9:40"` and car 12 at `"10:05"` — and sorts them with
+`key=lambda w: w["leaves"]`. That key is the raw string, so Python sorts
+`"10:05"` and `"9:40"` as strings, not as times. The output is car 12 (10:05)
+printed first, car 7 (9:40) second.
+
+For the quay command, `cli.py` calls `boards.quay_board(book)`. It filters to
+`end == "quay"` — car 3 at `"9:40"`, car 9 at `"10:05"` — and sorts with
+`key=lambda w: minutes_past(w["leaves"])`. `minutes_past` splits the string on
+`:`, converts both halves to `int`, and returns `hour * 60 + minute`: 580 for
+`"9:40"`, 605 for `"10:05"`. Sorting on those integers puts car 3 (9:40) first
+and car 9 (10:05) second — the order a clock would give.
+
+Same book, same day, same pair of times chalked the same way on each end —
+but the two boards run two different sort keys over them, and only one of
+those keys measures time.
+
+## Why it comes out that way
+
+- **`town_board` sorts on the string itself.** `boards.py` line 23:
+  `sorted(cars, key=lambda w: w["leaves"])`. Python's string ordering compares
+  `"10:05"` and `"9:40"` character by character: `"1"` (0x31) is less than
+  `"9"` (0x39), so `"10:05"` sorts before `"9:40"` regardless of what the
+  numbers mean. The docstring at the top of `boards.py` says this in the
+  shed's own terms: the town board "lists its cars by the written time, the
+  way the chalkboard reads" — it is explicitly a lexical read of the chalk,
+  not an arithmetic one.
+
+- **`quay_board` sorts on a computed minute count.** Line 29 sorts on
+  `minutes_past(w["leaves"])`, and `minutes_past` (lines 14–17) does the
+  arithmetic: split on `:`, `int(hour) * 60 + int(minute)`. That collapses
+  `"9:40"` and `"10:05"` to comparable integers, so the sort follows the
+  clock rather than the alphabet. The docstring gives the reason the two
+  boards differ at all: the quay board "went up two summers later, after the
+  quay men had words about where their early car sat" — it was built, later,
+  specifically to fix the ordering fault that `town_board` still has.
+
+- **`shedbook.enter` never normalizes the time it stores.** Line 34's own
+  docstring is explicit: "the time kept as chalked." `enter` only checks the
+  shape of the string (`hour.isdigit()`, two-digit minute) and then appends
+  it unchanged — no zero-padding, no conversion to a number. So `book.json`
+  holds `"9:40"`, one character shorter than `"10:05"`, and that raw string
+  is exactly what `town_board` sorts on. Nothing between the chalking and the
+  board printing ever pads `"9:40"` to `"09:40"`, which is the one change
+  that would have made the string order match the clock order.
+
+Put together: one shared, unpadded string representation of time; one board
+(`town`) that sorts that string as text; one board (`quay`) that sorts a
+number derived from it. The same two times, `9:40` and `10:05`, are bound to
+land in opposite orders whenever the hour lengths differ, and today they do.
+
+## Boundaries and edge behavior
+
+- **The fault is specifically about hour-length, not about quay being
+  "right" in general.** If every time chalked for an end happens to have
+  hours of the same digit-length (e.g. both two-digit, `"09:40"` and
+  `"10:05"`, or both single-digit, `"9:05"` and `"9:40"`), lexical and
+  numeric order agree, and `town_board` would look correct by accident. The
+  disagreement shown today is a property of this book's specific times (one
+  single-digit hour, one double-digit hour on each end) — it is not that
+  `town_board`'s method is sound and just mis-happened once; it's that its
+  method is unsound and today's data happens to expose it.
+
+- **`enter` enforces a shape, not a semantics, on the time.** It requires
+  `hour.isdigit()` and a two-digit minute, but places no bound on the hour's
+  value or digit count — `enter(book, 1, "town", "99:40")` or a three-digit
+  hour would be accepted and chalked exactly as given. The repository's own
+  comment ("nothing anywhere pads or trims it after") settles that this is
+  deliberate: the book is a record of what the foreman wrote, not a
+  normalized time value, and `town_board`'s ordering inherits whatever
+  irregularity that record contains.
